questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Since I major in Asian Studies with a focus on Japan it was only logical to apply for a university in Japan. Seeing as I intend to write my thesis on Japanese working cultures I thought it would be relevant to look at law and policy studies to better incorporate these academic fields.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The biggest obstacle I faced and lesson I learned in academic terms was that courses offered for Graduate students were dismally few in number and exclusively law classes. The acronyms "SS" and "FS" do not, in fact, stand for "Spring Semester" and "Fall Semester" but instead "Second Semester" and "First Semester", their first semester commencing in spring. All courses I had intended to take were therefore not available to me.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: All information was available on their online intranet named manaba. It was therefore easily accessible and was complimented by an orientation meeting before class start. Additional information was made available at the dormitories, but seeing as I did not obtain a room I had to forgo that.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There were several things that needed to be done, such as registering at the local city hall as a resident, getting your taxes and insurance calculated and send, registering for courses, etc. As a student making self-arranged accommodations I had to figure out most of it myself. The orientation meeting and continued assistance from their international office was a big help though.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: The international office was helpful and skilled English speakers. The lack of assistance in terms of registering at city hall was my own responsibility as my accommodations were self-arranged and therefore needed to take place at the corresponding city hall.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Besides dormitories, the school did not have other recommendations aside from the offical listings which were insanely expensive. Therefore, I searched through AirBnB and found a few places with reasonable prices. I warmly recommend the AirBnB in Musashimurayama hosted by Hagiwara Yoshitomo. It was cheap, within a doable distance of Tama campus and the host was friendly and very helpful, although if you do not speak Japanese it might get a bit challenging.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
Do not do it. If you can pay more than 5.000 dkkr pr. month in rent then there are accommodations within 30 minutes. But basically every exchange student lives at the dormitories and any person not residing there, student or not, barred from entering. Most of student life outside of classes will therefore take place without you. If you do choose to arrange accommodation yourself, double check the address of the campus you will study at. Tama campus of Chuo university is not, in fact, located in Chuo district. My mistake in this regard saw me mistakenly book a room at an AirBnB with 2hours and 45minutes of commute to school. I had luckily only book a single month and promptly changed address to Musashimurayama with a "mere" 1hour and 30minutes travel time. This, however, neccessitated a second and third trip to city hall, first to report that I was moving out of the district, then to report at the new district that I was moving in. It is neither a fun nor short experience. 
In terms of student life, it is not impossible to meet classmates and locals, with more chances to meet locals unaffiliated with school if you arrange your own living quarters. It is, however, limited in social events you can participate in as dormitories are inaccessible and camera surveilled. It is also exhausting to do do on top of classes and homework in combination with commuting.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I never entered a dormitory so I would not know. As far as I heard the IRC dormitory at campus was nice with a well-stocked kitchen and various leisure equipment. Unfortunately for the residents, due to incidents prior to my stay, alcohol consumption was not allowed which probably curbed parties from occurring to some degree. Seiseki was more free in terms of rules and came with individual bathrooms and showers as opposed to the former. It did require taking the bus for 20 minutes though.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: If, by registration, it refers to the process leading up to being admitted it was a lovely hell with several deadlines with no mercy for those missing them (it is worth noting the deadlines given are according to the Japanese time zone). If it refers to course selection, however, it was fairly lax with several opportunities to re-select classes during the first few weeks which students were recommended to make use of by surveying a few classes the first week before making their final choices.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Again, there is a stark difference between course selection and admittance procedure. The admittance procedure had 3-4 deadline clusters where various documents were required. It was a bit of a mess, whereas my own university forgot to notify me that I was nominated, so the first deadlines were uncomfortably close whilst it was too late for scholarship applications, hence my self-arrangement. Dormitory applications demanded that rent was paid in full for all 5 months in advance in cash, which I simply did not have. Course selection on the other hand was relaxed, albeit slow in updating. The syllabus provided was 2 years old with the relevant syllabus uploaded after the orientation meeting.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The dormitories provided ample assistance with registering at city hall, tours of the area, etc. Or so I have been told. Besides that, there was the orientation meeting as well as continued assistance by the international office. They were very helpful and despite having a rule written on their online page stating that students were required to apply for consultation ahead of time, I sort of forgot that and simply turned up unannounced. They always helped and never told me of the rule so I only noticed several months in.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Very unsuccessful. As mentioned, the syllabus that I had based my planning on was very different in course selection when it finally updated, the SS/FS acronym debacle destroyed my plans a second time with an even narrower course selection as several demanded that you attended from spring. In the end, due to having no prior knowledge in psychology and engineering, I had no choice in what courses to take to fulfill the ECTS requirements from home. Japanese language courses above a certain level demanded JLPT-certification to attend with all lower-standard classes remaining uncreditted for Graduate students. All language proficiency statements from my professors were therefore superfluous. I did attend Japanese classes as an audit student but all classes were in the mornings whilst my full courseload ensured my classes ran until 5PM most days. Admittedly, I did not have the energy to keep attending on top of my commute and other classes. Finally, all classes were legal classes aside from Public Administration with a professor with less attendance throughout the year than my personal "best". It was quite impressive, really.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: If you are a BA-student then there are a plethora of courses to take within several fields of study. If you are a Graduate student without a JLPT-certificate, then the courses are indirectly selected for you. There simply are no additional options if you wish to meet ECTS demands from home. Two classes can be chosen between as they lie in the same time slot, but aside from that I hope that you want to study law.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The lowered score is due to the sparse selection in my case. The classes themselves were interesting with (mostly) highly qualified professors that cover various facets of law at a level that still allows the uninitiated to keep up with law students.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level was high and competent but from a beginner's level so that students such as myself could follow.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The classes were mainly teacher-centered lectures with required readings provided on manaba and then discussed by the professor, typically with a case study in mind. Some classes aimed at student discussions, two actually had them. There were homework that required you turn in a very small essay or made a short presentation on a topic seen from your own country's perspective. Exams were manifold but pleasantly short compared to the length typically required at home.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
-Legal Systems in Major Foreign Countries (although it says 'major countries' it was exclusively based on the American Supreme Court)
-Japanese Law
-Law and Society (This was mainly based on student discussions in comparing differing views on these keywords from the countries of origin)
-Comparative Constitutional Law (Had several teachers, not all with understandable English but an interesting class nonetheless)
-Contemporary Challenges in the Law of the Sea (interesting but difficult course)
-Comparative Privacy and Data Protection Law (interesting class with a relaxed and humorous professor. Exam was integral to the classes and were therefore done before the exam period. Highly recommended to ease the exam period load. He also included segments in which he recommended places to go. He did not, however, know anything about technology).
-Public Administration
-Advanced Public Administration (PA was taught by the same professor. Advanced was necessitated by the fact that I did not have enough classes. I was the only participant in the latter and so she never convened a class. We had collectively 6 classes she did not cancel, she did not seem to want to be present and little to no information on exams were provided. I was ultimately told that a final paper for the advanced course were needed for a grade not the credit. As the deadline was simultaenous with the other course I elected to forgo writing it. I am now 2 credits short, to which I in no way harbor bitter feelings over)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
-Law and Society was heavily engaging for students with both exchange students and Japanese students attending. Discussions were the driving force where law and society were viewed from the standpoints of the nationalities represented in class.
-Comparative Constitutional Law were taught by the Vice Principal as well as other teachers at other points of time. As I have a personal interest in Japan's Constitutional Law and was one of the few classes I had intended to study before arriving, I was quite satisfied with the course. The English skills of the teachers varied, however, but was interesting even so.
-Comparative Data and Privacy Protection Law was relaxed in atmosphere, gave students free reign in choosing what they wanted to write about within the field, the exam was an essay and presentation which were written and presented throughout the course, freeing students for other exams. It also came with a cultural segment where the professor recommended places to visit.
Contemporary Challenges in the Law of the Sea was an interesting topic that dealt with current disputes addressed through UNCLOS. It dealt with many regions throughout the world and discussed challenges which are broadly relevant for all. It was, however, probably the hardest course that I took.

questions.question: Insurance DKK *
Housing DKK per month *
Books DKK per month *
Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *
Communication (phone, internet, etc.) DKK per month *
Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
-I lost my laptop in Shinjuku one month before exams started. Replacing it was expensive and unpleasant. I would advice anyone getting stuck mid-city with bulky belongings once trains stop running to make use of the coin lockers located at train stations.
-I wanted to acquire currency at Copenhagen Airport before departure and chose a vendor there. They promised an updated exchange rate with a small handling fee. I ended up losing 1.500 dkkr in said "low fee." Advice: If they ask you to sign a waiver before processing the transaction you are likely being scammed. ATM's can be found in all 7-11's in Japan with actual low fees.
-Japanese books ran for roughly 200dkkr pr. Had I not been an audit student it would have cost a pretty penny all books combined.
-Transportation is not cheap when added up.
"charge" at bars and restaurants is a fee for sitting down.
A manga cafe I slept at offered a fix price for 3 hours which I agreed to and paid. They did not call the room when time was over and instead called me 5 hours later. The bill was considerately high and forgetting my cell phone resulted in an additional cost to retrieve.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Alcohol and dining out is wonderfully cheap compared with Denmark. Giving you the bill after you are done, however, can get expensive if you are not careful. cell phones are cheaper and I would have bought one if not for losing my laptop. Coincidentally, laptops are not cheap.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Due to my long commute and long study hours I never joined a club. I either had class when clubs convened or I did not have the grit to spend 3 hours commuting to participate on my days off. They offered a wide selection though, and for the sake of a club named "toilet club" alone, I have chosen to rate it as a 4.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There were several clubs of a huge variety, although it is mostly written in Japanese for those that do not read it. There was a school festival and a student-arranged welcome party in Shibuya. The party cost 200dkkr to enter and apparently the drinks were 50dkkr after that. Advice: Buy a ticket for an all-you-can-drink-party in the vicinity and alternate between the two to make it worth the money. Again, keep in mind when the last train leaves.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Drinking. Japanese alcohol prices are cheap and a good way of talking with locals that get (sometimes overly) enthusiastic about talking with a foreigner if you speak even elementary Japanese.
Eating. Dining out is also cheap and of high quality. Specifically Mazesoba is highly recommended.
Wandering/hiking. The scenery is beautiful with many mountains surrounding the city. Besides nature, going to a random train station and simply wander around can be interesting with unusual sights befitting the largest city in the world.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I did not go that many places as I was chronically broke. Visit Shibuya for shopping, visit Shinjuku for serious drinking, visit Kamikitadai for drinking in close proximity to where you live. Check out Asakusa, and other than that. Look around. Too many places to see for anyone to cover it all.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Seeing as it was not my first trip to Japan it was easy enough. The trains stopping at midnight, however, gets me every time.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Live at a dormitory and participate in clubs. Take a course with a mix of Japanese and exchange students. Seeing as I lived outside of dormitories and am over 30 years of age I was more interested in socializing with locals outside of school. When arriving, I recommend staying at a hostel for at least a few days. It is agreat way of meeting students from other universities as well as unafilliated Japanese citizens.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Trains stopping at midnight. The times I was caught in the city until morning were 10 too many. Also, smoking areas are strictly adhered to and typically located either inside in a booth or outside with an accompanied roof, which defeats the point of avoiding toxic fumes in my opinion. Japanese hesitance to say what they are thinking in combination with my own occasional failings at picking up on subtle social cues.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer:
Drinking with random locals as well as friends I had made there. 
Mazesoba. Apparently it is a Taiwanese dish and not Japanese which is why it took me 4 months to locate as Japanese people do not know what it is. Still worth the wait.
Clean streets and people not being unneccessarily loud.
The polite and friendly attitudes in general.
Convenience stores that truly have verything from ATM's, decent prices, chargers to rent for phones, actual chargers for sale, and just about everything else, etc.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Get a dormitory room.
Get the full and instant insurance option for your plane ticket home.
Check and double check train schedules with all transit points recalculated. If google maps believe that you can change trains in Shinjuku in 5 minutes, do not trust it. That station is neverending with an unproven connection to Narnia.
-Bonus advice: Do not underestimate the power-level of 'strong zero'.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: If you are a Graduate student I sincerely hope you are deeply interested in law. Also, get a dormitory.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting new friends in places I did not expect. Realizing I lived within viewing distance of mt. Fuji when randomly looking to the horizon. Gaining a deeper understanding of Japanese law through my courses and the society outside of them. Also, and I can not stress this enough, Mazesoba.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Finding mazesoba. It was truly a long and arduous journey to find a place. Also, losing my laptop and having to replace it whilst surviving on SU. Finally, having my plane ticket home cancelled on me by the airline still no refund in sight. Writing 6 exams in two weeks.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Crime in Japan is famously low. That does not, however, mean that there is no crime. Tokyo is the largest city in the world and as such, you may potentially encounter anything, money scams being the most common.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
